A relaxation oscillation alternates slow build-up with fast release. Van der Pol introduced the term for self-oscillating electrical circuits [@vanderpol1926relaxation]. The standard example is his oscillator with strong nonlinearity [@strogatz2024nonlinear, Section 7.5].

## The Van der Pol oscillator for large $\mu$

The equation $\ddot x + \mu(x^2 - 1)\dot x + x = 0$ has negative damping for $|x| < 1$ and positive damping for $|x| > 1$. With $F(x) = x^3/3 - x$ and $y = \dot x/\mu + F(x)$ it becomes

$$
\dot x = \mu\bigl(y - F(x)\bigr), \qquad \dot y = -\frac{x}{\mu},
$$ {#eq-vdp-lienard}

which is the form in `amlab/odes_2d/van_der_pol.py` [@strogatz2024nonlinear, Section 7.5].

For $\mu \gg 1$, $\dot x$ is of order $\mu$ and $\dot y$ of order $1/\mu$. Away from the cubic nullcline $y = F(x)$ the trajectory jumps almost horizontally, in a time of order $1/\mu$. On the outer branches of the cubic it creeps slowly, in a time of order $\mu$. When it reaches a knee of the cubic ($x = \pm 1$) it jumps to the other branch.

## The period

Strogatz computes the period from the time spent on the slow branches. On a slow branch $y \approx F(x)$, so $\dot y = F'(x)\dot x = (x^2 - 1)\dot x = -x/\mu$. Integrating from $x = 2$ to $x = 1$ and doubling for the two branches gives

$$
T \approx 2\mu \int_1^2 \frac{x^2 - 1}{x}\,dx = (3 - 2\ln 2)\,\mu \approx 1.61\,\mu,
$$ {#eq-vdp-period}

with corrections that vanish relative to $\mu$ as $\mu \to \infty$ [@strogatz2024nonlinear, Section 7.5].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-relaxation
#| fig-cap: "Van der Pol oscillator for mu = 10. Left: limit cycle and cubic nullcline in the Lienard plane. Right: x(t), with slow drifts and fast jumps."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.odes_2d.van_der_pol import van_der_pol

mu = 10.0
sol = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, (0, 80), [2.0, 0.0], args=(mu,), method="LSODA",
                t_eval=np.linspace(0, 80, 8000), rtol=1e-8)
xs = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 300)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
ax1.plot(xs, xs**3 / 3 - xs, "b", lw=1, label="y = F(x)")
ax1.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[1], "k", lw=1)
ax1.set_xlabel("x")
ax1.set_ylabel("y")
ax1.legend(fontsize=8)
ax2.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], "k", lw=1)
ax2.set_xlabel("t")
ax2.set_ylabel("x")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Numerical check

Measure the period from upward zero crossings of $x(t)$ and compare with @eq-vdp-period.

```{python}
for mu in [5.0, 10.0, 20.0, 40.0]:
    t_end = 12 * mu
    s = solve_ivp(van_der_pol, (0, t_end), [2.0, 0.0], args=(mu,), method="LSODA",
                  t_eval=np.linspace(0, t_end, 40000), rtol=1e-8)
    x = s.y[0]
    up = s.t[1:][(x[:-1] < 0) & (x[1:] >= 0)]
    period = np.mean(np.diff(up[1:]))
    print(f"mu = {mu:4.0f}: T = {period:6.2f}, (3 - 2 ln 2) mu = {(3 - 2 * np.log(2)) * mu:6.2f}")
```

The relative error falls as $\mu$ grows, as expected for an asymptotic formula.

## Where you meet it again

The FitzHugh-Nagumo model has the same geometry: a fast variable with a cubic nullcline and a slow recovery variable ([FitzHugh-Nagumo Model](fitzhugh-nagumo.qmd)). When its fixed point sits on the middle branch, the system produces relaxation oscillations; when it sits on an outer branch, the system is excitable.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise
Evaluate the integral in @eq-vdp-period.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$\int_1^2 (x - 1/x)\,dx = [x^2/2 - \ln x]_1^2 = (2 - \ln 2) - 1/2 = 3/2 - \ln 2$. Multiplying by $2\mu$ gives $(3 - 2\ln 2)\mu$.
:::
